_why: A guard is proven by breaking the thing it guards and watching it go red. This project does that
and writes what the guard said into the commit message - which is real, and one-time. It cannot be
re-executed. A guard proven in one month and quietly hollowed out in the next looks exactly like a
guard that still works: the suite is green either way.
This ledger is those proofs, kept as data. Each plant is the exact text substitution that puts the
defect back, and the suite that must go RED when it is there. tools/guard/replant.py applies one,
requires the named suite to fail, restores the file byte-for-byte and verifies the restore.
THREE RATCHETS, and every one of them may only fall.
owed                 registered suites with no plant at all - the honest size of what this
ledger does not cover.
owed_generalisation  plants marked site_only: the defect was put back at exactly the place it
was found, and nothing shows the guard would catch it somewhere else.
owed_real_defect     suites whose ONLY plant is marked auto. tools/guard/autoplant.py finds
those by mutating a line and watching the suite go red, which proves the
suite is not vacuous - a real thing to know, and NOT the same claim as a
hand-written plant, where the text put back is a defect that actually
happened to a user. Kept apart so a machine-generated line can never be
mistaken for the proof it is standing in for.
PlantLedgerTest holds all three to their ceilings and checks every plant still matches its file
exactly once, which is cheap; replant.py actually runs them, which is not.

plants.why: Where the centred grid image starts inside the panel was written out three times in three files, identically, and the input router had to re-derive it in screen coordinates because there was nowhere to ask. plants.why: The matrix cursor translates a point on the grid into a cell, and the multitude/sub-chunk tool makes that grid four times finer in each axis. plants.why: The NPC form wrote the zone and then re-read its script from that zone - and threw away the boolean saying whether the write had happened. One truncated region therefore took the whole editor down - from a browser whose entire job is to look at regions one after another, so it would have been found by the first person who scrolled past a bad one. Found by the guard, not by them. THE FIRST TWO DRAFTS OF THIS PLANT SURVIVED, and that was the useful part. The fix originally had two halves - this length-and-magic check and a catch on OutOfMemoryError - and each covered every input a suite could build, so neither could be proven while the other stood. No buffer could be constructed that passed the check and still ran away, so the Error catch was speculation, and speculation that cannot be tested or safely removed is worse than none. It was deleted; this check is the whole fix, and it proves. The must_say is the section wrapper's own sentence rather than a check line: an OutOfMemoryError is not a failed assertion, it is the section dying, and what this plant proves is precisely that the editor would die. The wrapper catches Throwable so it is reported rather than taking the whole battery quietly. SURVIVED TWO FULL RUNS (2026-09-20 and 2026-09-21), because NOTHING DROVE IT: it reddened some other section incidentally when written, and once that stopped being true it proved nothing while the ledger still counted it. decode() is public, static and GL-free precisely so a suite can ask - and nobody asked until aRegionThatWillNotDecodeAnswersNothing.

retired.why: The dropdown preview reaches the row the user is ON through the combo box's popup list, and the only way to that list is the UI delegate's accessible child being a BasicComboPopup. Guessing that the accessible child IS the list - the obvious simplification, and wrong - makes popupList answer null. Nothing throws: attach returns false, no listener is added, and the dropdown opens with no preview beside it and no complaint anywhere. That is word for word what the owner reported about the version before this one ("still zero zone preview"), so the feature's one fragile dependency is also the one whose failure is invisible. The check looks for the hook rather than trusting it. RETARGETED: the bubble window this was written against is gone - it broke the owner's standing rule that a feature lives in its own part of the UI, and it was invisible to them twice. What survived is the hook itself, in ComboHighlight, feeding the preview panel that now sits in the Zone Loader tab. The claim is unchanged: lose the popup list and the preview silently stops following the row being arrowed through.
retired.retired: 2026-09-13: the code this claim was about is gone. It guarded the hook that read the Load Zone dropdown's popup list, which existed so a preview could follow the highlighted row. The dropdown is not how zones are picked any more - the Zone Loader has a list you arrow through with the preview beside it - so ComboHighlight was deleted as unreachable. A claim whose subject no longer exists cannot be retargeted onto anything honest; it is kept here so the history of what was once proven is not quietly shorter than it was.

retired.why: Four anonymous threads, one per movement key, each looping on whether its key was still held and each swallowing the InterruptedException that exists to stop it - and none of them daemons. A key press whose release never arrives (a focus change, a modal dialog, the window closing) left one walking the camera for the life of the process, holding the 3D panel alive and keeping the JVM up after the last window closed. There is one thread now, it is a daemon, and it honours the interrupt. This swallows it again, which also puts the silent-catch count back up over its ceiling - the two are the same defect seen from two sides.

retired.retired: 2026-10-08: the code this claim was about is gone. The camera walker was a daemon thread whose InterruptedException this plant swallowed; F016 made it a Swing Timer on the event thread, because the thread wrote the camera the mouse handlers write. There is no thread to stop and no catch to swallow. The claim that replaced it - the camera does not walk on a thread of its own - is the-camera-walks-on-a-thread-of-its-own-again.
